title: The Most Terrifying Warriors Ever
fullText: This is Mimizuka, a small burial mound in the middle of the Japanese city of Kyoto. Inside lie the ears and noses of 70,000 people, and it was the samurai who buried them. The year is 1597. This is a battlefield between Japanese and Korean forces. Samurai walk through the wounded, looking for ears and noses to cut off. Later, they pack them into barrels of salt and bring them home as trophies. The more they brought back, the greater the honor. In video games and movies, we're used to the image of a noble warrior. But in reality, a samurai could kill a peasant with no consequences, just to test how sharp their katana was. For 700 years, they ruled Japan and essentially created the world's first military dictatorship. And even when the Japanese finally got rid of them, samurai traditions lived on. In the 20th century, those traditions transformed Japan into a brutal empire that only two atomic bombs could stop. But then out of those ashes, one of the most successful countries in the world was born. And here's the idea. None of it would have been possible without those same samurai traditions. Because the history of Japan is in many ways the history of the samurai. And what you're about to hear is that story told as if it all happened yesterday. Take a look at the map. This is the late 8th century. At this point, Japan is still a relatively small island state. The largest islands are Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu. The country is ruled by an emperor who sits in the capital. Hango, known today as Kyoto, is regarded as a living god. from the rest of the world. Japan is separated by the ocean. Naval technology is still limited, so no one is really able to reach or invade it. Because of this, the emperor doesn't need a large standing army, but warfare still continued. In Japan, food is scarce and large areas of land remain undeveloped. On the northern part of Honu Island and on Hokkaido Island live the Amishi. These are ancient tribes who were there even before the Japanese. The Amishi hunt, fish, and conduct raids. Meanwhile, the Japanese view them with hostility and consider them barbarians. Because these barbarians do not recognize the emperor's authority and refuse to allow the Japanese into their lands, the emperor decides to form a military force to bring them under control. He gathers peasants and trains them up as soldiers. But the results are disappointing. In the north, the climate is far too harsh for them. And on top of that, the Amish trained in warfare since childhood, while ordinary peasants stand little chance against them. That's why the emperor decides to send into battle those who had no place in his capital, his younger sons. There are great many of them, far more than you can expect. He could have dozens or even hundreds of concubines who continuously give birth to children. And for all of them, there was no inheritance. So, the emperor grants them lands in the north and tells them that all they need to do is conquer them. In return, they'll receive glory, a new home, and exemption from taxes. Alongside them, sons of provincial nobility are also sent north, known as Kundai warriors. Provincial governors along the border also begin forming their own self-defense units. This mix of forces sparks a conflict with the Emishi tribes. Each commander gathers a small unit around themselves, around 50 to 100 people. They're also promised a share of the lands they conquer. A strange arrangement given that they were granting land that wasn't even theirs. In short, the members of these units served their commanders. Essentially, these are the first samurai, although the term didn't exist yet. These early warriors were highly motivated, as they were promised significant rewards. They trained intensely and learned to fight from the ground up. Their primary weapon became the bow, not the katana we're used to seeing in films. They shot from horseback at high speed with remarkable accuracy. They were so precise that when the Emishi captured samurai prisoners, they would sever the tendons in their arms to prevent them from ever drawing a bow again. After the bow, the second most important weapon for these warriors was the spear. As for the katana, which would appear much later, it was used only rarely. In the end, the samurai slowly begin to defeat the enemy tribes. Other Japanese people hear about these victories, and new volunteers head north, hoping to get land of their own. The Emishi are pushed farther and farther north. The samurai who would stand out most in battle begin forming their own clans. On the lands they reclaimed, they build fortifications and hire peasants to grow rice. And that's how they get rich. Soon peasants start leaving imperial lands on their own and going to work for samurai estates instead. They don't really care who they pay taxes to. What matters is who protects their harvest. So in the end, everyone benefits. Everyone except the emperor of Japan that is. But he doesn't understand this and starts granting land not only to his descendants but also to aristocrats. This is how the emperor tries to secure their loyalty. These aristocrats also become samurai. By the 12th century, samurai clans control half of Japan. The emperor has no real power over them because he still doesn't have his own army. Meanwhile, the samurai clans own fields and produce their own rice. And with that rice, they hire more and more soldiers into their forces. At one point in Japan, rice even functioned as currency. Samurai became used to solving every problem with force until they began fighting not just the emishi but each other as well. At first they clash over small things, a piece of land or the right to collect taxes. But over time the stakes grow. The samurai clans become so wealthy that they start fighting for influence over the emperor himself. One of these clans was the Tida clan. They placed their own people into key positions in the capital. The clan's leader, Tyra Noki, openly controlled the emperor and even arranged for his daughter to marry into the imperial family. But the Tyra were opposed by the Minamoto clan. The Minamoto were fierce northern samurai who had fought against the Emishi, and the Minamoto deeply resented the fact that the Tyra were seizing power behind their backs. So war broke out between them and the Minamoto lost. The leader of the Minamoto clan, Minamoto no Yori Masa is surrounded in a temple. He refuses to surrender. So while his servants hold off the Titer forces, Yorim Masa writes a short poem on his fan, then sits down and disembowels himself. From this poetic legend, a samurai tradition is born. Ritual suicide known as sepuku. In other words, the samurai either dies in battle or takes his own life. After Yorimasa's sepuku, the Tyra kill all the adult men of the Minamoto line. Only the children are spared. Among them is 14-year-old Minamoto Nooritomo. He's sent into exile on a distant island where he spends 20 years. During this time, the Tyra clan expands its power even further as the emperor of Japan becomes the grandson of Tyra Nokiomorei, 5-year-old Antoku. And now the clan sets its sights on controlling all of Japan. The smaller samurai clans are obviously not happy about this. They have no intention of giving up their lands. And these dissatisfied samurai rally around a descendant of the Minamoto clan, the same Yoritomo. This is how a new war begins, the Genee war, which lasts 5 years. Everything is decided in a naval battle at the bay of Don Noura in 1185. The Minamoto ships collide with the Tyra fleet and the battle begins. As it becomes clear that the Tyra are losing, their samurai jump into the water rather than be taken alive. They drag Minamoto warriors with them or grab onto heavy objects and sink beneath the waves. At that time, on one of the Taido ships was the young emperor of Japan, Antoku. When his grandmother saw that the battle was lost, she picked him up and jumped into the sea with him. This is an event that changes the course of Japan history forever. So, the Minamoto clan comes out on top. Soon in 1192, the new emperor appoints Minamoto Nooritomo as the great Shogun, conqueror of the barbarians. Yoritomo himself establishes a samurai government. And this marks the beginning of the shogunit period when all power in Japan shifts into the hands of the samurai. Some of them stop being just ordinary warriors. But who exactly is in charge of Japan during this time? In short, no one and everyone. At the same time, the emperor no longer makes decisions. From then on, his role was to pray and devote himself to the arts. Real power shifts to the shogun, the commander-in-chief of the samurai army. Formally, he answers to the emperor, but in reality, he appoints officials and controls the military himself. Below him are the daniel, leaders of individual samurai clans. Each of them controls their own land, their own castle, and their own small army. They swear loyalty to the shogun and carry out his orders. Next come the bushi, ordinary samurai who either have no land at all or only very little. They serve their dou and have the right to collect taxes in his villages. And at the very bottom are ordinary people, farmers, artisans, and merchants. In theory, it all looks simple. The shogun is supposed to rule Japan. But in reality, this system almost never works the way it's meant to. But in practice, shoguns can't fully hold on to power and depend heavily on influential samurai clans. And the lower level daimo simply don't care about state affairs. They fight their neighbors or battle the Emishi to the north. Japan as a single unified state basically didn't exist at this point. In addition, samurai during this period were far from what we imagine today. The noble warrior who writes poetry and is ready to die at any moment that's either a movie character or a rare exception. Most samurai were brutal, often uneducated killing machines. And if their daimo suddenly lost power, a samurai could easily switch sides to a stronger lord or simply run away to save his life. Samurai who fled, betrayed their lord, or lost their master were expected to commit sepuku. If a samurai refused to take his own life, he became a ronin, a wandering warrior. Ronin traveled all across Japan looking for work. Most of them ended up as hired assassins or bandits. But there were rare cases where these warriors managed to preserve their honor. You might have heard of the film 47 Ronin starring Keanu Reeves. This story is based on real events. It happened much later than the period we're in right now, but it perfectly illustrates what a ronin actually is. It all began with a dispute between the heads of two samurai clans. Inside the castle of one of them, the other draws his katana. This violated the etiquette of the time, and whether or not he actually struck anyone doesn't matter. By law, such an act meant death. The clan leader is ordered to preserve his honor by committing sepuku. He agrees and disembowels himself. But he had 47 samurai in his service who argued the sentence was unjust. They agreed that their lord had indeed broken the law, but they argued he'd been provoked by the other clan leader. So he too should be required to commit sepuku. No one supported that idea. So the 47 samurai become ronin. They scatter across the country drinking and living recklessly. But the leader of the opposing clan still fears revenge. He sends spies to them and they report back that the ronin have already forgotten everything. Their leader is even found drunk in a ditch while a farmer spits on his face. After hearing this, the clan leader finally relaxes. But it soon turns out that the Ronin were only pretending. Some of them were secretly watching the clan leader and preparing their revenge. One winter night, during a heavy snowstorm surrounding his castle, the 47 Ronin quietly break inside. They kill the guards, find the clan leader, and tell him to commit sepuku. He refuses. So the Ronin behead him themselves, take his head to the grave of their master, and then surrender to the authorities. After a long trial, they're granted the honor of dying as samurai, and all of them publicly disembowel themselves. The Japanese believed that a person's life force resided in the abdomen. So by cutting open the stomach, a samurai was, in a sense, releasing his soul in front of everyone. But the sepu ritual didn't end there. The samurai's assistant was expected to immediately behead him. This was done so that in the final moments of life, a person would not show suffering in front of others and so that a samurai's head would not fall into enemy hands because it was considered a trophy. See, after battles, samurai would collect the heads of their enemies and present them to their commanders as proof of their strength. In return, they were rewarded with land and honor. That's why samurai who performed sepeku would appoint an assistant whose job was not only to behead them but also to hide the head so it can never be found because after death they did not want to become someone's trophy. For a samurai glory was sometimes more important than the battle itself. Their deeds had to be witnessed by others. If a samurai died in battle it had to be confirmed. And if he won he had to prove it by presenting the severed head of his enemy. no witnesses, no proof, no reward. There were even cases where samurai returned from battle without a single scratch, but also without any enemy heads, and then they'd have to go to court and prove that they actually fought and didn't simply just run away. Because of this, some samurai even painted their horses in bright colors so they could be easily seen during battle. And later, their participation could be verified. But not everyone was willing to risk their lives like that. So, some resourceful samurai would kill unarmed villagers and bring their heads as proof of their victories. Meanwhile, in wars between samurai clans, the rules were completely different. There were no largecale battles because, simply put, no one could feed large armies. Usually, only a few dozen samurai fought on each side, and at most a few hundred. And often, everything was decided by a duel between just two samurai. Here's how it worked. The armies would stand facing each other. Two samurai would step into the center and begin a ritual introduction. They would name all their ancestors that they could remember, recall any defeated enemies, and praise their clan. If it turned out that one of them wasn't famous enough for battle, the fight simply wouldn't happen. The defeat was considered automatic. But by the end of the 13th century, this tradition starts to fade. And the reason was the Mongols. At that same time, the grandson of Genghaskhan, Kublakhan, sends envoys to the Japanese islands for negotiations. At that time, the Mongol Empire had already conquered half of Asia, including China and Korea. And now its target was Japan. But there was a problem. The Mongols were not great at naval warfare. They didn't want to build a fleet or fight at sea. It simply wasn't their strength. So, Kublan sent envoys to the emperor with an ultimatum. Japan must either voluntarily accept the authority of the great Khan or the Mongols would come and take it by force. The emperor replied that he did not handle such matters and sent the envoys to the shogun in another city. The Mongols are stunned by this response. How could the emperor not make decisions? But they moved on anyway. Still, it changed nothing because the shogun completely ignored the envoys, leaving them no choice but to declare war. The Mongols together with their Korean vassels assembled a fleet of several hundred ships. In 1274, they arrived in Japan, captured several small islands, and landed on the shores of Kyushu. The Japanese, who were used to small battles and duels, sent 100 of their best samurai to negotiate with the Mongols. They were supposed to arrange a duel between Japanese and a Mongol warrior. The Mongols let them in, then surrounded them and shot them down with arrows. The main samurai army standing at a distance watched as their best warriors were wiped out in minutes. It was a strong start for the Mongols, but then problems began to appear. Their supplies of arrows and food quickly ran out. Transporting supplies and horses by sea was difficult, and without them, the army couldn't hold out for long. On top of that, the samurai began mounting strong defenses and prevented the Mongols from capturing Japanese fortresses. So, the Mongols withdrew. After this war, the samurai realized their swords were ineffective. They were too thin and often broke when striking heavy armor. So, the Japanese decided to completely rethink their design. Experiments in the 15th century eventually led to the creation of the katana. It was a light, extremely sharp sword, often weighing under a kilogram. Samurai treated katanas like living beings. They gave them names and passed them down through generations as priceless family heirlooms. Larger swords also appeared, the Odachi. They could be over 2 m long. They were wielded by the strongest samurai, who in full armor could intimidate enemies just by their presence. By the way, such armor is easy to recognize. It's all because of a special helmet, the Kabuto. Its shape is protected against arrows and overhead strikes. As for the main armor, it consists of metal plates connected with silk cords. This made it flexible. Samurai could move freely, shoot a bow, and fight with a katana. These silk cords also dampened the sound of clashing metal, allowing a samurai to move more quietly and strike by surprise. But putting on this armor required help from several servants because the main fastenings were on the back. The armor came in different colors since samurai often painted it. Red was meant to intimidate enemies. Blue protected the silk cords from fading in the sun. And white armor was worn by warriors who intended to die in battle. Separately, samurai also wore a cloak that was sewn and inflated with air. It formed strange balloon-like shapes that helped protect the back from arrows. In short, the Mongols left and the shogunit celebrated victory. But a few years later, Kublcon again sent envoys to Japan demanding surrender. This time they weren't even received. They were executed immediately. The Mongols prepared a second invasion. Inside the shogunit, plans were made to unite Japan for the coming war. A military reform began. Samurai from different clans were merged into larger armies. On Kyushu, the island closest to the mainland. Mandatory military service was introduced. Every warrior had to serve there for 3 months each year. Patrol units appeared along the coastline. Workers were forced to build fortifications and peasants were taxed to fund the army. The samurai state was finally unified. Japan was ready for war. In 1281, the Mongols returned with thousands of ships built by conquered peoples. This army consisted of two main parts. The first were ships from Korea and the second from China. And this is where problems began for the Mongols. The Chinese ships were delayed for up to 6 months because their crews kept falling ill. The Korean fleet couldn't wait that long and launched the attack on its own, but they were not allowed to land. The samurai once again organized a strong defense. A short time later, the Chinese ships finally arrived, but they didn't change the situation. Most of the soldiers on board were Chinese, forced into service by the Mongols, so many surrendered in mass, and the rest were smashed against the rocks by a massive typhoon. The Mongols were defeated once again and never attempted to invade Japan again. The samurai believed they'd been protected by the gods themselves. The typhoon was named Kamakaz, meaning divine wind. During the wars of the Mongols, samurai from different clans unite for the first time in history. Seems like Japan is finally on the path to becoming a single unified country. But instead, a far greater chaos begins. Samurai clans from the south claim they deserve the newly conquered lands the most. And that makes sense since they took the hardest hit. But the shogun backs not them, but the older samurai clans from the north who once gained fame fighting the Emishi. But even for them, there still isn't enough land because there's almost no free territory left. Out of the major islands, only Hokkaido remains unconquered. As a result, the clans begin arguing even more and once again turn their weapons on each other. Japan becomes increasingly brutal. Ritual duels are no longer practiced. Rice production expands and now it is enough to support large armies. Single battle can now involve 5,000 to 10,000 warriors. The shogun loses the last remnants of real power. Now neither he nor the emperor actually makes decisions. Power belongs to whoever has the strongest army. Samurai actually welcome these changes because war is what they live for. Their status becomes untouchable. They're allowed to kill someone of lower rank if that person insults them in any way. At one point, it isn't even punished, but instead it's encouraged as a way to test the sharpness of their katana. In short, Japan is thrown into extreme chaos and its peak arrives in 1467. That's when the era of non-stop war begins. Sangoku Jidai, the age of waring states. Japan at the time looks like this. Every small piece of land is its own independent region that obeys no one. And for more than a hundred years, they fight each other nonstop. And what makes this even more interesting is that the first Europeans arrive in Japan at the same time. In 1543, a storm carries a Portuguese ship to the islands. At first, the Portuguese try to trade with the Japanese, but the local population is poor, so the only thing that really interests them are smaller silver deposits. Meanwhile, the Japanese are drawn to Portuguese weapons. They take two Aquabuses from them, take them apart, and spend 13 years trying to replicate them. Eventually, Japanese craftsmen not only copy the weapons, but improve them. Japan begins mass-producing its own version, the Tanagashima. By the end of the 16th century, it's already found in every army. But this new weapon doesn't sit well with the samurai. They claim a true warrior should not use it because it is dishonorable. On top of that, the early firearms were less accurate than bows and sometimes even exploded in the user's hands. But in reality, the samurai had a different reason. For many years, they trained exclusively with spears, bows, and katanas. Not just anyone can fight with these weapons, which meant power belonged only to them. And now, a weapon appears that anyone can learn to use in just a few days. And a simple farmer who just yesterday could be cut down by a katana can now defend himself. Because of this, most samurai refused to use firearms, and soon they begin losing to those who do not reject the new weapons. Perhaps the one who understood the true power of firearms best was Oda Nounaga, a warlord determined to unify Japan. Nounaga does not rely only on samurai in his army. He arms farmers with guns, turning them into Ashu infantry. His tactic is simple. Farmers fire and while they reload, samurai with bows cover them. This brings Nobunaga repeated victories. For ordinary people, a path into the military hierarchy suddenly opens up. One farmer even rises all the way up to become a general. His name was Tayatomi Hidoshi. He started from the very bottom. Hidoshi was Nabonaga's servant and at first he even carried his sandals. Over time, he is given increasingly difficult tasks and eventually becomes the most important figure in Nabonaga's army. Hidoshi helps him in battles against two major enemies. The first warrior Buddhist monks. In medieval Japan, monasteries had their own armies and heavily fortified strongholds. And monks controlled key trade routes. The most powerful among them were the monks of the Ecoeki sect. They preached that all people are equal before Buddha and organized peasant uprising against the samurai. And this directly stood in the way of Nobunaga's goal of unifying Japan. So he decided to attacked their monastery near Kyoto Hongji. It was a true fortress from which the monks controlled the surrounding lands. In the past, samurai clans avoided attacking monks believing it would anger the gods. But Abunaga did not hesitate. His army surrounds the monastery, breaks through, and wipes out all the monks. The second enemy of Nabunaga is the province of Ega, the birthplace of the ninja. Samurai had already been defeated there several times because the ninja fought a guerilla war, hiding in forests, striking without warning, and disappearing again. But Nabunaga comes up with a different strategy. He divides his forces into five groups that attack the province from different directions at the same time. They kill everyone they encounter, men, women, and children. The entire province is wiped out. Nabunaga now seems unstoppable. He's taking control of more than half of Japan. But in 1582, one of his own generals, Akachi Mitsuhide, betrays him and suddenly attacks the temple where Nabonaga is staying overnight. Realizing what is happening, Nabunaga commits Sepuku. Tayatotoi Hidoshi, the same loyal servant who once started at the very bottom, quickly learns of his master's death. He immediately sends his army against Mitsuhide, crushes his forces, and Mitsuhide himself is killed while fleeing. And just like that, a former peasant begins to rule Japan. But because of his background, Hidoshi cannot become shogun. That title can only be held by aristocrats. So he declares himself Imperial regent. In practice, he rules the entire country and continues the process of unifying Japan. Hidoshi bans samurai clans from fighting each other and begins building a professional standing army while also prohibiting common peasants from becoming samurai just as he once did. On top of that, he raises taxes. These measures don't sit well with the population, and rebellions begin breaking out across different provinces. In response, Hidoshi orders all weapons to be confiscated from everyone except the samurai. In some villages, even sickles and sides are taken away. They're only handed back during harvest season and then locked away again in special storehouses. This is how unarmed martial arts began to emerge in Japan. 300 years later, they will influence the development of judo, karate, and iikido. Despite all of this unrest, Hideoshi's harsh laws do produce results. Almost all of Japan is fully unified and wars between clans come to an end. But the massive samurai armies still remain and they need something to do. So Hidoshi sends them to conquer Korea and China. In 1592, a massive Japanese army of roughly 150,000 warriors lands in Korea. It defeats Korean forces and quickly takes control of the country. And this is where the samurai become their most brutal. After battles, they once again cut off the heads of their enemies and send them back to Japan to prove their victory to Hidoshi. But over time, there are so many heads that there's simply no space left on the ships. So, the samurai begin cutting off the enemy's noses and ears instead. These are packed into barrels of salt and shipped back to Japan. There, they're counted and used to assign additional rewards to the samurai. Then, the question arises, where do you even put all of this? The samurai come up with a solution. They build burial mounds where all these ears and noses are buried. This is why the mound you saw at the beginning of the video has two names. Hanuzuka, mound of noses, and Mimizuka, mound of ears. But the Koreans still refuse to give up and begin waging guerrilla warfare against the samurai. Soon, Chinese forces also come to assist the Koreans. Japan is facing even bigger problems now. But Hidoshi isn't being told any of this because everyone fears his reaction. So he believes that Japan is on the verge of victory. To put this into perspective, at one point the Chinese emperor sends envoys to Japan. They arrive and offer Hideoshi the chance to wear ceremonial Chinese clothing. Hidoshi thinks, "Great, this means they're admitting defeat." And happily agrees. But later, he finds out that it actually meant accepting surrender terms. By that time, the samurai army was already exhausted. Over 6 years of war in Korea, 80,000 warriors had died. In the end, they returned home with nothing. When Hidoshi was already in his 50s, his health and mental state began to fail. His condition collapsed after illness and the failed invasion of Korea. On top of that, he faced a succession crisis since his wife was infertile. Hidoshi, of course, had his own harum, but for some reason, his concubines only gave birth to daughters. Towards the end of his reign, his 16-year-old concubine finally gives birth to a son, but he dies almost immediately. Surprisingly, the same 16-year-old concubine later gives Hidoshi another son. Soon after, the aging ruler creates a special council of five of the most powerful samurai in Japan, meant to govern the country until his son comes of age. Eventually, in 1598, Hidoshi dies, and these five samurai, unsurprisingly, immediately turn on each other and start a war. The winner is Tokugawa Yayausu, one of Hidoshi's old generals. He finally completes the unification of Japan and establishes his own shogunit named after the new capital Edo. Today that city is Tokyo. Tokugawa starts employing foreigners into his service. The first is a Dutchman, Yang Yusten, a merchant who becomes an official adviser to the shogun. The second and far more famous is an Englishman William Adams. In 1600, his ship was wrecked off the coast of Japan. Adams is taken before Tokugawa and he impresses him so much with his knowledge of ship building. The Tokugawa hires him for life. Adams is given the Japanese name Mura Anjin along with an estate and the status of a samurai. He builds powerful European style ships for the Japanese, marries a Japanese woman and spends the rest of his life there. Today, Tokyo even has a district named after William Adams Ajin Cho. His story was even turned into a novel called Shogun, which was later adapted into a TV series not too long ago. In the end, these two advisers helped push Tokugawa towards expelling Catholic Christians from Japan because they themselves were Protestants. Later, the Shogun expels all Europeans from the country entirely. And this is how Japan effectively closes itself off from the rest of the world. Hokugawa stops waging wars with other countries. The samurai no longer know what they're supposed to do. Some enter government service. Others turn to the arts, writing poetry and painting. And some simply drink their days away. For many samurai, life in the new Japan becomes difficult. They long for the time when the country was constantly at war. Out of this nostalgia, the Bushido code emerges. From Japanese, the way of the warrior. It's a collection of rules describing the ideal samurai. Honest, fearless, loyal, and ready for self-sacrifice. And even though in reality most samurai lived by completely different principles, the Bushidto code still becomes popular. And today we imagine samurai exactly in that way. By the mid-9th century, Japan feels almost frozen in time. While the rest of the world is building factories and industrial cities, the country of the samurai still lives as it did 300 years earlier, growing rice and fishing. This continues until 1853 when American ships arrive and force Japan to open its ports for trade. Later, the Europeans do the same. The Edeto Shogunut try to push them out, but it cannot because both the Japanese army and navy are already outdated. Japan falls under western influence. For the first time, Japanese people travel to Europe and see highly developed cities. Compared to them, Tokyo looks like a large village. So, they return home, determined to modernize their country. Japan begins copying Western clothing, buying modern weapons, and adopting foreign laws. One group of samurai support these changes. Another demands that foreigners be expelled and traditions preserved. Because of this, a civil war breaks out among the samurai. Those who support westernization rise up against the Edoshogunit. They want to restore real power to the emperor and modernize the country. These rebels win because they have modern weapons and military advisers from the United States, France, and Germany. The last shogun from the Tokugawa family transfers power to the young emperor Miji. The emperor begins to rule alongside a pro-western government. He completely reforms the country, equalizing the rights of peasants and samurai. Ordinary Japanese people gain the right to travel freely across the country and choose their own professions. In 1872, a decree is issued to create a regular army modeled after western standards. For the samurai, these reforms mark the end of their high social status. Especially painful is the ban on wearing katanas and traditional samurai hairstyles. Soon, samurai also lose their government stipens and are forced to find other work. As a result, several uprisings break out. The first was the Kamicaz League rebellion. 174 samurai attack the Imperial Army, but are quickly defeated. 86 rebels commit sepoku while the rest are executed by local authorities. A year later, a much larger uprising begins, the Satsuma Rebellion. It is led by the popular samurai Saigo Takamorei who is highly respected amongst the aristocracy. The emperor respects Takamorei because he previously helped destroy the Edeto shogunits. So he is reluctant to declare him a traitor and that turns out to be a mistake because the rebels actually have a real chance of winning. They seize an arsenal of modern weapons and fight better than the new Japanese army. Saigo Takamorei plans to take Tokyo and force the emperor to restore the samurai's rights. The rebels begin marching towards the capital. Along the way, they attack Kumamoto Castle, defended by only 4,000 newly recruited soldiers. But the siege drags on. Imperial forces arrive just in time to support the defenders with Western artillery. The siege is lifted and the rebels begin to fall back. The decisive battle takes place on September 24th, 1877. The remaining forces of Takamorei's samurai army, running out of ammunition, launch a final assault. 500 samurai with katanas, charge at 30,000 soldiers armed with rifles. Saigo Takamorei dies alongside his men. The Satsuma rebellion is crushed. Thousands of samurai are executed or sent into exile on the island of Hokkaido. But their story does not end there. The samurai who supported the emperor go on to become businessmen, politicians, or even military officers. Có lúc, nó thậm chí còn không bị trừng phạt mà thay vào đó nó được khuyến khích như một cách để kiểm tra độ sắc bén của thanh katana của họ. Nói tóm lại, Nhật Bản rơi vào tình trạng hỗn loạn tột độ và đỉnh điểm là vào năm 1467. Đó là khi kỷ nguyên chiến tranh không ngừng nghỉ bắt đầu. Sangoku Jidai, thời đại chiến quốc. Nhật Bản vào thời điểm đó trông như thế này. Mỗi mảnh đất nhỏ là một khu vực độc lập riêng, không tuân theo ai. Và trong hơn một trăm năm, họ chiến đấu với nhau không ngừng nghỉ. Và điều khiến điều này trở nên thú vị hơn nữa là việc những người châu Âu đầu tiên đặt chân đến Nhật Bản cùng thời điểm. Năm 1543, một cơn bão cuốn tàu Bồ Đào Nha đến quần đảo. Lúc đầu, người Bồ Đào Nha cố gắng buôn bán với người Nhật, nhưng người dân địa phương nghèo nên điều duy nhất họ thực sự quan tâm là những khoản tiền gửi bạc nhỏ hơn. Trong khi đó, người Nhật lại bị thu hút bởi vũ khí của Bồ Đào Nha. Họ lấy hai chiếc Aquabus ra, tháo chúng ra và dành 13 năm cố gắng để nhân rộng chúng. Cuối cùng, các thợ thủ công Nhật Bản không chỉ sao chép vũ khí mà còn cải tiến chúng. Nhật Bản bắt đầu sản xuất hàng loạt phiên bản của riêng mình, Tanagashima. Đến cuối thế kỷ 16, nó đã có mặt ở mọi đội quân. Nhưng loại vũ khí mới này không phù hợp với samurai. Họ cho rằng một chiến binh thực thụ không nên sử dụng nó vì nó là điều ô nhục. Hơn hết, các loại súng cầm tay thời kỳ đầu kém chính xác hơn cung tên và đôi khi thậm chí còn phát nổ trên tay người dùng. Nhưng trên thực tế, các samurai lại có lý do khác. Trong nhiều năm, họ được huấn luyện hoàn toàn bằng giáo, cung và katana. Không phải ai cũng có thể chiến đấu bằng những vũ khí này, điều đó có nghĩa là sức mạnh chỉ thuộc về them. Và bây giờ, một loại vũ khí xuất hiện mà bất cứ ai cũng có thể học cách sử dụng chỉ trong một vài ngày. Và một người nông dân giản dị mới hôm qua đã có thể bị chém bởi một thanh katana bây giờ có thể tự vệ. Vì điều này, hầu hết samurai từ chối sử dụng súng và chẳng bao lâu họ bắt đầu thua cho những người không từ chối vũ khí mới. Có lẽ người hiểu rõ nhất sức mạnh thực sự của súng ống chính là Oda Nounaga, một lãnh chúa quyết tâm thống nhất Nhật Bản. Nounaga không chỉ dựa vào samurai trong quân đội của mình. Anh ta trang bị súng cho nông dân, biến họ thành bộ binh Ashu. Chiến thuật của anh ấy rất đơn giản. Nông dân bắn và trong khi họ nạp đạn, samurai với cung tên sẽ che chắn cho họ. Điều này mang lại cho Nobunaga những chiến thắng liên tiếp. Đối với những người bình thường, một con đường vào hệ thống cấp bậc quân sự đột nhiên mở ra. Có nông dân thậm chí còn vươn lên thành tướng quân. Tên anh ấy là Tayatomi Hidoshi. Anh ấy bắt đầu từ tận đáy. Hidoshi là người hầu của Nabonaga và lúc đầu anh ấy còn mang cả dép của mình. Theo thời gian, anh được giao những nhiệm vụ ngày càng khó khăn và cuối cùng trở thành người quan trọng nhất nhân vật trong quân đội của Nabonaga. Hidoshi giúp anh trong trận chiến chống lại hai kẻ thù lớn. Những tu sĩ Phật giáo chiến binh đầu tiên. Ở Nhật Bản thời trung cổ, các tu viện có quân đội riêng và các thành trì kiên cố. Và các nhà sư kiểm soát các tuyến đường thương mại quan trọng. Người quyền lực nhất trong số họ là các tu sĩ của giáo phái Ecoeki. Họ rao giảng rằng mọi người đều bình đẳng trước Đức Phật và tổ chức cuộc nổi dậy của nông dân chống lại samurai. Và điều này đã trực tiếp cản trở mục tiêu thống nhất Nhật Bản của Nobunaga. Vì vậy ông quyết định tấn công tu viện của họ gần Kyoto Hongji. Đó là một pháo đài thực sự mà từ đó các tu sĩ kiểm soát các vùng đất xung quanh. Trong quá khứ, các gia tộc samurai tránh tấn công các nhà sư vì tin rằng điều đó sẽ chọc giận các vị thần. Nhưng Abunaga không hề do dự. Quân đội của ông ta bao vây tu viện, đột phá và tiêu diệt tất cả các tu sĩ. Kẻ thù thứ hai của Nabunaga là tỉnh Ega, nơi sinh của ninja. Samurai đã bị đánh bại vài lần ở đó vì ninja chiến đấu với quân du kích chiến tranh, trốn trong rừng, tấn công không báo trước và lại biến mất. Nhưng Nabunaga lại nghĩ ra một chiến lược khác. Ông chia lực lượng thành 5 nhóm tấn công tỉnh từ nhiều hướng khác nhau cùng một lúc. Họ giết tất cả những người họ gặp, đàn ông, phụ nữ và trẻ em. Toàn bộ tỉnh bị xóa sổ. Nabunaga bây giờ dường như không thể ngăn cản được. Ông ta đang nắm quyền kiểm soát hơn một nửa Nhật Bản. Nhưng vào năm 1582, một trong những vị tướng của chính ông, Akachi Mitsuhide, đã phản bội ông và bất ngờ tấn công ngôi đền nơi Nabonaga ở qua đêm. Nhận ra điều gì đang xảy ra, Nabunaga phạm tội Sepuku. Tayatotoi Hidoshi, người đầy tớ trung thành từng bắt đầu từ đáy, nhanh chóng biết về cái chết của chủ nhân mình. Anh ta lập tức phái quân đi đánh Mitsuhide, đè bẹp lực lượng của hắn, còn chính Mitsuhide thì thiệt mạng khi bỏ trốn. Và cứ như thế, một cựu nông dân bắt đầu cai trị Nhật Bản. Nhưng vì xuất thân của mình nên Hidoshi không thể trở thành tướng quân. Danh hiệu đó chỉ có quý tộc mới có thể nắm giữ. Vì vậy, ông tự xưng là nhiếp chính của Hoàng gia. Trên thực tế, ông cai trị toàn bộ đất nước và tiếp tục quá trình thống nhất Nhật Bản. Hidoshi cấm các gia tộc samurai chiến đấu với nhau và bắt đầu xây dựng vị thế chuyên nghiệp quân đội đồng thời cấm nông dân bình thường trở thành samurai giống như ông đã từng làm. Trên hết, anh ta còn tăng thuế. Những biện pháp này không được lòng người dân và các cuộc nổi dậy bắt đầu nổ ra khắp các tỉnh khác nhau. Đáp lại, Hidoshi ra lệnh tịch thu tất cả vũ khí của mọi người ngoại trừ samurai. Ở một số làng, thậm chí liềm và sườn cũng bị lấy đi. Chúng chỉ được trao lại trong mùa thu hoạch và sau đó được nhốt lại trong nơi đặc biệt nhà kho. Đây là cách võ thuật không vũ trang bắt đầu xuất hiện ở Nhật Bản. 300 năm sau, họ sẽ ảnh hưởng đến sự phát triển của judo, karate và iikido. Bất chấp tất cả tình trạng bất ổn này, những luật lệ khắc nghiệt của Hideoshi vẫn mang lại kết quả. Hầu như toàn bộ Nhật Bản đã được thống nhất hoàn toàn và các cuộc chiến tranh giữa các gia tộc đã đi đến hồi kết end. Nhưng đội quân samurai đông đảo vẫn còn tồn tại và họ cần phải làm gì đó. Vì vậy Hidoshi cử họ đi chinh phục Hàn Quốc và Trung Quốc. Năm 1592, một đội quân khổng lồ của Nhật Bản gồm khoảng 150.000 chiến binh đổ bộ vào Hàn Quốc. Nó đánh bại lực lượng Hàn Quốc và nhanh chóng nắm quyền kiểm soát đất nước. Và đây là lúc các samurai trở nên tàn bạo nhất. Sau trận chiến, họ một lần nữa chặt đầu kẻ thù và gửi họ quay trở lại Nhật Bản để chứng minh chiến thắng của mình với Hidoshi. Nhưng theo thời gian, có quá nhiều cái đầu đến nỗi không còn chỗ trống trên những con tàu. Vì vậy, các samurai bắt đầu cắt mũi và tai của kẻ thù. Những thứ này được đóng gói vào thùng muối và chuyển về Nhật Bản. Ở đó, chúng được tính toán và sử dụng để trao thêm phần thưởng cho các samurai. Sau đó, câu hỏi đặt ra là bạn đặt tất cả những thứ này ở đâu? Các samurai đưa ra một giải pháp. Họ xây dựng những ngôi mộ nơi chôn cất tất cả những chiếc tai và mũi này. Đây là lý do tại sao gò đất bạn nhìn thấy ở đầu video có hai cái tên. Hanuzuka, gò mũi và Mimizuka, gò tai. Nhưng người Triều Tiên vẫn không chịu bỏ cuộc và bắt đầu tiến hành chiến tranh du kích chống lại samurai. Ngay sau đó, lực lượng Trung Quốc cũng đến hỗ trợ quân Triều Tiên. Nhật Bản hiện đang phải đối mặt với những vấn đề thậm chí còn lớn hơn. Nhưng Hidoshi không được kể bất cứ điều gì về điều này vì mọi người đều lo sợ phản ứng của anh ấy. Vì vậy ông tin rằng Nhật Bản đang trên đà chiến thắng. Để dễ hình dung, có lúc hoàng đế Trung Quốc cử sứ giả đến Nhật Bản. Họ đến và cho Hideoshi cơ hội mặc trang phục nghi lễ của Trung Quốc. Hidoshi nghĩ, "Tuyệt, điều này có nghĩa là họ đang thừa nhận thất bại. " Và vui vẻ đồng ý. Nhưng sau đó, anh ấy phát hiện ra rằng điều đó thực sự có nghĩa là chấp nhận các điều khoản đầu hàng. Vào thời điểm đó, đội quân samurai đã kiệt sức. Hơn 6 năm chiến tranh ở Triều Tiên, 80.000 chiến binh đã thiệt mạng. Cuối cùng, họ trở về nhà mà không có gì. Khi Hidoshi đã ngoài 50, sức khỏe và trạng thái tinh thần của ông bắt đầu fail. Tình trạng của ông suy sụp sau bệnh tật và cuộc xâm lược Triều Tiên thất bại. Hơn hết, anh còn phải đối mặt với cuộc khủng hoảng kế vị vì vợ anh bị vô sinh. Tất nhiên, Hidoshi có harum riêng nhưng không hiểu sao chỉ có thê thiếp sinh được con gái. Đến cuối triều đại của ông, người vợ lẽ 16 tuổi của ông cuối cùng cũng sinh ra một con trai, nhưng anh ta chết gần như ngay lập tức. Điều đáng ngạc nhiên là sau đó chính người vợ lẽ 16 tuổi đó lại sinh cho Hidoshi một đứa con trai khác. Ngay sau đó, người cai trị già thành lập một hội đồng đặc biệt gồm năm người samurai quyền lực ở Nhật Bản, có nhiệm vụ cai trị đất nước cho đến khi con trai ông ta lên ngôi age. Cuối cùng, vào năm 1598, Hidoshi qua đời, và không có gì đáng ngạc nhiên khi năm samurai này ngay lập tức phản đối mỗi người. khác và bắt đầu một cuộc chiến. Người chiến thắng là Tokugawa Yayausu, một trong những vị tướng cũ của Hidoshi. Cuối cùng ông đã hoàn thành việc thống nhất Nhật Bản và thành lập tướng quân của riêng mình mang tên thủ đô mới Edo. Ngày nay thành phố đó là Tokyo. Tokugawa bắt đầu tuyển dụng người nước ngoài vào làm việc cho mình. Đầu tiên là một thương gia người Hà Lan Yang Yusten trở thành cố vấn chính thức tới tướng quân. Người thứ hai và nổi tiếng hơn nhiều là người Anh William Adams. Năm 1600, con tàu của ông bị đắm ngoài khơi Nhật Bản. Adams đã bị bắt trước Tokugawa và anh ấy đã gây ấn tượng mạnh với anh ấy bằng kiến ​​thức của mình của việc đóng tàu. Tokugawa thuê anh ta suốt đời. Adams được đặt tên tiếng Nhật là Mura Anjin cùng với tài sản và địa vị của một samurai. Anh ta đóng những con tàu mạnh mẽ kiểu châu Âu cho người Nhật, kết hôn với một phụ nữ Nhật Bản và dành phần còn lại của cuộc đời mình ở đó. Ngày nay, Tokyo thậm chí còn có một quận được đặt theo tên của William Adams Ajin Cho. Truyện của ông thậm chí còn được chuyển thể thành tiểu thuyết có tên Shogun, sau này được chuyển thể thành một bộ phim truyền hình cách đây không lâu. Cuối cùng, hai cố vấn này đã giúp thúc đẩy Tokugawa tiến tới việc trục xuất những người theo đạo Công giáo khỏi Nhật Bản vì bản thân họ là người theo đạo Tin Lành. Sau đó, Tướng quân trục xuất toàn bộ người châu Âu ra khỏi đất nước. Và đây là cách Nhật Bản tách mình ra khỏi phần còn lại của một cách hiệu quả thế giới. Hokugawa ngừng tiến hành chiến tranh với các nước khác. Các samurai không còn biết họ phải làm gì nữa. Một số tham gia dịch vụ của chính phủ. Những người khác chuyển sang nghệ thuật, làm thơ và vẽ tranh. Và một số chỉ đơn giản là uống rượu trong những ngày xa cách của họ. Đối với nhiều samurai, cuộc sống ở Nhật Bản mới trở nên khó khăn. Họ khao khát thời kỳ đất nước thường xuyên có chiến tranh. Thoát khỏi nỗi nhớ này, mật mã Bushido xuất hiện. Từ tiếng Nhật, con đường của chiến binh. Đó là tập hợp các quy tắc mô tả samurai lý tưởng. Trung thực, không sợ hãi, trung thành và sẵn sàng hy sinh bản thân. Và mặc dù trên thực tế hầu hết các samurai đều sống theo những nguyên tắc hoàn toàn khác nhau, Bushidto mã vẫn trở nên phổ biến. Và ngày nay chúng ta tưởng tượng samurai chính xác theo cách đó. Vào giữa thế kỷ thứ 9, Nhật Bản cảm thấy thời gian gần như bị đóng băng. Trong khi phần còn lại của thế giới đang xây dựng các nhà máy và thành phố công nghiệp thì đất nước của các samurai vẫn sống như 300 năm trước, trồng lúa và câu cá. Điều này tiếp tục cho đến năm 1853 khi tàu Mỹ đến và buộc Nhật Bản phải mở cảng để buôn bán. Sau này người châu Âu cũng làm như vậy. Tướng quân Edeto cố gắng đẩy họ ra nhưng không thể vì cả Quân đội và hải quân Nhật Bản đã lỗi thời. Nhật Bản rơi vào ảnh hưởng của phương Tây. Lần đầu tiên, người Nhật đi du lịch châu Âu và ngắm nhìn những thành phố phát triển cao. So với họ, Tokyo trông giống như một ngôi làng lớn. Vì vậy, họ trở về quê hương, quyết tâm hiện đại hóa đất nước. Nhật Bản bắt đầu sao chép quần áo phương Tây, mua vũ khí hiện đại và áp dụng luật pháp nước ngoài. Một nhóm samurai ủng hộ những thay đổi này. Một yêu cầu khác là trục xuất người nước ngoài và bảo tồn truyền thống. Vì điều này, một cuộc nội chiến nổ ra giữa các samurai.
